pharm: 4-aminoquinoline antimalarial and immunomodulatory antirheumatic agent used for malaria, rheumatoid arthritis, and lupus

summary: Hydroxychloroquine sulfate is a 4-aminoquinoline antimalarial and antirheumatic agent indicated for treatment of uncomplicated malaria (P. falciparum, P. malariae, P. ovale, P. vivax), prophylaxis of malaria in chloroquine-sensitive areas, and treatment of rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, and chronic discoid lupus erythematosus in adults. It is given orally with food or milk, with chronic maintenance doses generally not exceeding 200-400 mg daily. Its most characteristic toxicity is irreversible retinal damage related to cumulative dose and treatment duration, mandating a baseline ophthalmologic examination and periodic (annual) monitoring. Other serious risks include fatal cardiomyopathy and QT prolongation/ventricular arrhythmias, severe hypoglycemia, hematologic toxicity, and hemolysis in G6PD deficiency. It has a very long terminal half-life (about 40-50 days), so onset of effect and resolution of toxicity are slow.

moa: Hydroxychloroquine is a 4-aminoquinoline. As an antimalarial, it concentrates in the acidic food vacuole of intra-erythrocytic Plasmodium parasites, raising intravesicular pH and interfering with the parasite's ability to detoxify heme (inhibiting heme polymerization to hemozoin), which is toxic to the parasite. The mechanisms underlying its anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory effects in rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, and chronic discoid lupus erythematosus are not fully known but are thought to involve accumulation in lysosomes with increased pH, interference with antigen processing and presentation, and inhibition of toll-like receptor signaling, dampening autoimmune inflammatory responses.

relative: Porphyria (may worsen; hepatotoxicity reported in porphyria cutanea tarda) - avoid
Congenital or acquired QT prolongation or risk factors for QT prolongation
Hepatic disease or use with hepatotoxic drugs
monitor: Ophthalmologic examination - baseline and periodic (BCVA, visual field, SD-OCT)
Muscle strength and deep tendon reflexes (myopathy/neuropathy)

preg: Prolonged clinical experience over decades and available published epidemiologic and clinical data have not identified a drug-associated risk of major birth defects, miscarriage, or adverse maternal or fetal outcomes with hydroxychloroquine use in pregnancy. There are risks to mother and fetus from untreated or active malaria, rheumatoid arthritis, and systemic lupus erythematosus during pregnancy. Animal reproduction studies were not conducted. A pregnancy exposure registry monitors outcomes (1-877-311-8972). Use when needed for the maternal condition.
lact: Published lactation data report that hydroxychloroquine is present in human milk at low levels. No adverse reactions, and no retinal, otologic, cardiac, or growth/developmental abnormalities, have been reported in breastfed infants exposed through breast milk. There is no information on effects on milk production. Weigh the developmental and health benefits of breastfeeding against the mother's clinical need and any potential adverse effects on the infant.
renal: Renal clearance of unchanged hydroxychloroquine accounts for approximately 16% to 30% of the dose. Renal impairment is a risk factor for retinal toxicity, and reduced clearance may increase exposure; use with caution and consider dose reduction in renal impairment. Monitor for proteinuria and renal toxicity (phospholipidosis can contribute to renal injury, particularly in connective tissue disorders); discontinue if renal toxicity is suspected or demonstrated.
hepatic: Use with caution in patients with hepatic disease or alcoholism, or in those taking known hepatotoxic drugs. Hepatotoxicity has been reported, including in patients with porphyria cutanea tarda (in whom the drug should be avoided). Monitor liver function in patients with hepatic impairment.

major: QT-prolonging / arrhythmogenic drugs - increased risk of ventricular arrhythmias; hydroxychloroquine is not recommended with these agents
Insulin and other antidiabetic drugs - hydroxychloroquine may enhance their effect and increase hypoglycemia risk; a dose decrease of the antidiabetic agent may be needed
Drugs that lower the seizure threshold (e.g., mefloquine and other antimalarials) - increased seizure risk
moderate: Cyclosporine - increased plasma cyclosporine levels; monitor levels closely
Digoxin - may increase serum digoxin levels; monitor levels closely
Cimetidine - 2-fold increase in chloroquine exposure (interaction with hydroxychloroquine cannot be ruled out); avoid concomitant use
Methotrexate - may increase the incidence of adverse reactions
Antiepileptic drugs - their activity may be impaired
minor: Rifampicin - lack of hydroxychloroquine efficacy reported; avoid concomitant use
Praziquantel - chloroquine reported to reduce praziquantel bioavailability
interactions.food: Administer with food or milk to improve tolerability; food does not meaningfully reduce efficacy.
interactions.alcohol: Limit alcohol because of additive risk of hepatotoxicity.
interactions.diagnostics: May cause hypoglycemia (measure blood glucose if symptoms occur); monitor CBC for cytopenias; obtain baseline and periodic ophthalmologic testing and ECG for QT.

serious: Irreversible retinal toxicity / maculopathy (dose- and duration-related)
QT prolongation and ventricular arrhythmias (including torsades de pointes)
Hematologic toxicity (bone marrow depression, agranulocytosis, aplastic anemia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia)
rare: Serious skin reactions (Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, DRESS, acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis)
emergency: Torsades de pointes / ventricular fibrillation / cardiac arrest

monitoring: Baseline ophthalmologic examination within the first year of therapy - best corrected distance visual acuity, automated threshold visual field of the central 10 degrees (central 24 degrees in patients of Asian descent), and spectral domain OCT (SD-OCT)
Periodic ophthalmologic exams - annual screening for higher-risk patients; for those without risk factors, annual exams can usually be deferred until 5 years of treatment
ECG / QT interval, especially with cardiac disease or concomitant QT-prolonging drugs
Blood glucose, particularly if symptoms of hypoglycemia
Complete blood count periodically for hematologic toxicity
Muscle strength, deep tendon reflexes, and signs of neuropathy/myopathy with prolonged use
Mood and behavior for neuropsychiatric reactions
counsel: Take with food or milk; do not crush or divide tablets

Get a baseline eye exam and regular follow-up eye exams - retinal damage can be permanent and is related to how much and how long you take the drug; report any change in vision, difficulty reading, light sensitivity, or distorted/missing areas of vision
Report symptoms of low blood sugar (shakiness, sweating, confusion, palpitations); diabetic patients should monitor blood sugar, as doses of insulin or diabetes medicines may need lowering
Report fainting, palpitations, or irregular heartbeat (heart rhythm risk)
Report fever, sore throat, unusual bleeding/bruising, severe rash with blistering or peeling, or muscle weakness
For malaria prevention, take exactly on schedule - 2 weeks before travel, weekly during, and 4 weeks after; use additional mosquito-avoidance measures
Keep out of reach of children - overdose can be rapidly fatal, especially in children
Tell your doctor about all medicines, especially other QT-prolonging drugs, diabetes medicines, digoxin, cyclosporine, or methotrexate
pk: Antimalarial action prompt; antirheumatic effect is cumulative and may take several weeks to months
Whole-blood Tmax about 3.3 hours (plasma Tmax about 3.7 hours); oral bioavailability about 74-79%
Terminal half-life approximately 40-50 days in whole blood
Once-weekly (malaria prophylaxis) to daily dosing; extensive tissue distribution; renal clearance accounts for ~16-30% of dose
Store at 20-25 C (68-77 F); excursions permitted 15-30 C (59-86 F) (USP controlled room temperature)
pearls: Retinal toxicity is the signature risk - it is irreversible and related to cumulative dose and duration; keep daily dose <=5 mg/kg actual body weight and obtain baseline plus periodic ophthalmologic monitoring (BCVA, visual field, SD-OCT)
In patients of Asian descent, retinopathy may first appear outside the macula - test the central 24 degrees of the visual field rather than the central 10 degrees
Can cause fatal cardiomyopathy and QT prolongation/torsades - avoid in QT prolongation or with other arrhythmogenic drugs and do not exceed the recommended dose
Can cause severe hypoglycemia even without antidiabetic drugs; check glucose if symptoms occur and reduce antidiabetic doses as needed
Very long half-life (~40-50 days) means slow onset of antirheumatic benefit and slow resolution of toxicity after discontinuation
Screen for G6PD deficiency risk (hemolysis) and avoid in psoriasis and porphyria; overdose is rapidly life-threatening, particularly in children
missed: For weekly malaria prophylaxis, take the missed dose as soon as remembered, then resume the regular weekly schedule. For daily rheumatologic dosing, take the missed dose when remembered unless it is near the next dose, in which case skip it and resume the usual schedule. Do not take a double dose to make up for a missed one.
overdose: Overdose is dangerous and can be rapidly fatal, especially in children, with symptom onset within 1-3 hours of ingestion. Reported effects include cardiovascular toxicity (QRS/QTc prolongation, ventricular tachycardia, ventricular fibrillation, torsades de pointes, AV block, cardiac arrest, death), life-threatening hypotension, severe hypokalemia from intracellular shift, and CNS depression, seizures, visual disturbances, transient blindness, and coma. Manage with supportive and intensive care; consider gastrointestinal decontamination within the first hour (secure the airway first if consciousness is deteriorating), monitor and manage plasma potassium, and treat arrhythmias. Hemofiltration, hemodialysis, and hemoperfusion are not of benefit. Contact a poison center (1-800-222-1222) or medical toxicologist.
